# Tool Design as API Design {#sec-tool-design}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** The measurements run `qwen3.5:9b` through
`ollama` 0.24.0 at temperature 0, one pass per condition, n = 60 per cell.
`ollama` does not grammar-constrain enum values in a tool definition, so the
enum measured below is a hint the model reads, not a decoding constraint —
which changes what the result means, and is spelled out where it matters.
Nothing is executed in the schema experiment — it scores the *call* the model
emits, so the model's arithmetic cannot contaminate a result about schemas. @sec-agent-anatomy owns the loop; this chapter owns what the
loop reaches for. Software: NumPy 2.5.2 on Python 3.14.5.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- write tool schemas a model uses correctly on the first try, and say which
  part of the schema did the work;
- design error messages a model can recover from, and measure whether it does;
- decide what a tool should return, and what it must never return;
- keep a large tool surface usable, and know when to stop adding tools.

## The description is prompt text {#sec-tool-design-schema}

A [**tool schema**](#gloss-tool-schema){#term-tool-schema .term-ref} looks
like documentation and behaves like a prompt.

::: {#gloss-tool-schema .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Tool schema** — the name, description, types and enums a model sees before
choosing a call. Prompt text rather than documentation, because the model gets
one shot from it and cannot check a guess.
[↩](#term-tool-schema){.term-back}
:::

That single sentence is the chapter; everything below follows from it.

The distinction matters because the two are written by different instincts.
Documentation is written for a reader who can ask a colleague, read the source,
or try it and see.

[A model gets one shot, from the schema alone, with no way to check.]{.hl} It
cannot open your codebase. It cannot see an example call. Whatever the schema
does not say, the model guesses — and a guess that type-checks is
indistinguishable from an understanding.

So the schema carries four separate jobs, and it is worth being able to name
which one you are doing:

| the field | the job it does |
|:--|:--|
| **name** | tells the model *when* this tool applies, before it reads anything else |
| **description** | resolves the cases the name leaves ambiguous, and rules out the ones it should not be used for |
| **parameter types and enums** | put your API's own vocabulary in front of the model — and, *if your runtime constrains decoding*, make out-of-set values unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged. Which of the two you get depends on your stack, not on your schema — @sec-decoding |
| **parameter descriptions** | carry the mapping from how a user phrases a thing to what your API calls it |

: Four jobs, one object {tbl-colwidths="[30,70]"}

The last row is the one people skip, and it is where most misuse comes from.
Your users say *how much was set aside for it*; your API calls it `budget_allocated`.
Something has to bridge that, and if the schema does not, the model invents a
bridge.

**What we will look at.** First a measurement of which part of a schema
actually earns its keep, where the answer is uncomfortable for anyone who has
spent an afternoon polishing a tool description. Then the same treatment
applied to error strings, which produced the largest single effect measured in
this chapter — and where the raw exception most tools return by default turns
out to be a half-written error message. Then what a tool should hand back, which is a
question about the agent's memory rather than about output. Then what to do
when there are too many tools to list at all. And finally how to tell whether a
tool is any good, which is not a question you can answer without asking a
model.

### Measured: which part of the schema does the work?

Four versions of one tool, differing only in how they are described. The task
is to fetch one numeric field about a project, and the questions **never name
the field literally** — *how much money was allocated* has to become
`alan="butce"`. So the schema is the only thing that can carry the mapping.
Nothing is executed; what is scored is the call the model emits.

Two of the four differ by four words. Here they are in full:

```json
// variant B — named, free string
{"name": "veri_getir",
 "description": "Fetch one field of one project.",
 "input_schema": {"type": "object",
   "properties": {"proje": {"type": "string"},
                  "alan":  {"type": "string"}},
   "required": ["proje", "alan"],
   "additionalProperties": false}}

// variant C — the only change is the enum
{"name": "veri_getir",
 "description": "Fetch one field of one project.",
 "input_schema": {"type": "object",
   "properties": {"proje": {"type": "string"},
                  "alan":  {"type": "string",
                            "enum": ["butce", "personel", "sure"]}},
   "required": ["proje", "alan"],
   "additionalProperties": false}}
```

Variant A replaces every name with `f1`, `a`, `b` and empties the description;
variant D is C plus a written-out `description` on each parameter.

```text
qwen3.5:9b, 60 questions, one tool, four descriptions
95% intervals are Wilson on n = 60

 variant         called a tool  project right  field right   95% CI          fully correct
 A. opaque               58.3%           0.0%         0.0%   [ 0.0,   6.0]            0.0%
 B. named               100.0%         100.0%        25.0%   [15.8,  37.2]           25.0%
 C. enum                100.0%         100.0%       100.0%   [94.0, 100.0]          100.0%
 D. described           100.0%         100.0%       100.0%   [94.0, 100.0]          100.0%
```

[Listing the accepted values did all of the measurable work.]{.hl} Going from
free strings to an enumerated list took field accuracy from **25% to 100%** —
15/60 against 60/60 on the *same* 60 requests, so the data are paired and
McNemar is the test. Because variant C got every request right, the pairing is
forced: 45 requests improved and none got worse, and exact McNemar gives
$p = 2 \times 2^{-45} \approx 5.7 \times 10^{-14}$. (An earlier draft quoted
Fisher's $p < 10^{-19}$, which treats the variants as independent samples: the
conclusion is the same, the number is not.) Careful prose descriptions on top
of the enum added **nothing observable** — though with C already at 60/60 there
was no room left to add anything. That is the opposite of where most effort
goes: people write the description and leave the parameter as a string.
The paired test is what the close comparisons later in the chapter need, and it
is what you should run on your own tool.

**What the enum is doing here, and what it is not.** `ollama` does not
grammar-constrain enum values in a tool definition, so variant C's 100% is not
the decoder refusing to emit `mali buyukluk`. It is the model reading `butce,
personel, sure` in the schema and using them. That matters, because it makes
this finding and the error-message finding later in the chapter the *same*
finding: what fixed both was putting the API's vocabulary where the model could
see it. If your runtime *does* constrain decoding — hosted APIs call this a
schema-enforced or `strict` mode (@sec-decoding) — the enum becomes a
guarantee and this experiment tells you nothing about the model at all. Say
which case you are in before you generalise.

**And one cell is missing — the one that decides how far this generalises.**
The four variants are a ladder, not a factorial: nothing → names → names +
enum → names + enum + prose. The untested rung is *names + prose, no enum*.
Without it, the honest statement is not "prose does nothing" but "prose adds
nothing **once the enum has already put your vocabulary in front of the
model**". For a parameter you cannot enumerate — a free-text query, a date, an
id, an open-ended filter — a description is the only bridge you have, and this
experiment says nothing about it. Read rule 3 below as an argument rather than
a measurement.

Two rows deserve their own explanation, because each teaches something the
totals hide.

**The opaque schema did not make wrong calls. It made no calls.** With a tool
named `f1` taking `a` and `b`, the model called it 58.3% of the time and,
when it did not, answered from parametric memory (what it absorbed in training)
instead — inventing a
paragraph about what `ZRG-14` supposedly is. That is a far worse failure than a
malformed call: a wrong call errors, and an invented answer looks like an
answer.

**Without the enum, the model echoes the user's vocabulary into your API.**
Here is the whole of variant B, one row per phrasing:

```text
  MISS  wanted butce     got "bütçe"           ← "ne kadar para ayrildi?"
  MISS  wanted butce     got "mali buyukluk"   ← "mali buyuklugu nedir?"
  OK    wanted personel  got "personel"        ← "kac kisi calisiyor?"
  MISS  wanted personel  got "ekip mevcudu"    ← "ekip mevcudu nedir?"
  OK    wanted sure      got "sure"            ← "kac ay suruyor?"
  MISS  wanted sure      got "takvim"          ← "takvimi ne kadar?"
```

Neither of the two it got right contains the API's word: *kac kisi calisiyor*
has no `personel` in it, and *kac ay suruyor* has no `sure`. There the model
mapped the meaning — how many people, how many months — onto a field name, and
the name it chose was the API's own. Everywhere else it passed the question's vocabulary
straight through — *mali buyukluk*, *ekip mevcudu*, *takvim*. The model is not
guessing badly; it has no way to know that your API says `butce`, so it says
what the user said.

And note the first row, which is @sec-turkish-nlp arriving in a new place: the
model wrote **`bütçe`** where the API expects **`butce`**. Correct Turkish,
wrong identifier. Any API whose parameter values are ASCII-folded versions of
real words has this failure waiting in it, and an enum removes it here.

Not everywhere, though, and the difference is worth being precise about. An
enum in a schema is a hint your model usually follows; normalising at the tool
boundary is a guarantee you control. Do both: apply NFC, then fold diacritics
through an explicit alias table (`bütçe → butce`) *before* you validate. And
never round-trip an identifier through `.lower()` without a locale —
`"IŞIK".lower()` is `işik`, not the Turkish `ışık`, and `"İSTANBUL".lower()`
picks up a combining dot. Accept what the model plausibly sends; store what your API needs.
@sec-turkish-nlp has the rest of the traps; this is the one that reaches your
function signature.

::: {.fig-cap}
The four phrasings variant B got wrong. In every one the model passed the
user's own word into the parameter, because nothing in the schema told it what
the API calls that field. The first row is the sharpest case: `bütçe` is
correct Turkish and a wrong identifier.
:::

::::

::: {.column-margin}
The honest scope: one model, one tool, three fields. And note what the ladder
does and does not establish: it shows that putting the API's vocabulary in the
schema is worth far more than describing it in prose *on top of* that. It does
not rank constraints against prose in general, because the prose-only rung was
never run. What generalises is that the vocabulary has to reach the model
somehow — not the exact numbers, and not an ordering the design cannot see. A larger model
might infer `butce` from context; a schema with twelve fields would make the
enum matter more, not less. Run the variant sweep on your own tools; it is an
afternoon and it is the highest-yield afternoon in this chapter.
:::

### So write schemas in this order

The measurement gives an ordering, and it is roughly the reverse of the one
most people follow.

1. **Enumerate everything enumerable.** Every parameter with a fixed value set
   becomes an `enum`. This is the change with the measured effect.
2. **Name the tool for when it applies**, not for what it wraps. `find_orders`
   over `db_query_orders`.
3. **Write the parameter description as a mapping**, from the words users use
   to the value your API wants: *butce = the money allocated*.
4. **Then** write the tool description, for the cases the name leaves open —
   including what the tool is *not* for, which is the part that stops a model
   reaching for it wrongly.
5. **Make optional parameters rare.** Every optional parameter is a decision
   the model has to make with no information, and a default you did not
   document is a guess it will make differently each time.

## Error messages are prompts {#sec-tool-design-errors}

The line marked 6 in @sec-agent-anatomy's loop turned an exception into an
observation. That makes
the error string prompt text too — the model reads it and decides what to do
next — and almost nobody writes it that way, because error messages are written
for a human who will be reading a log.

The claim is testable. Hold everything fixed and change only what the tool
returns when it fails. To make every condition face exactly the same failure,
the first tool call is rejected **unconditionally**, whatever the model asked
for; the score is on the *second* call. One artefact comes with holding the
string fixed: a model that sent `butce` correctly is still told that `'bütçe'`
was invalid. That keeps the four conditions comparable, which is the point,
but every condition is slightly less coherent than a real error would be, and
the traceback condition — which quotes the value — suffers most from it.

```text
qwen3.5:9b, 60 tasks, first call always rejected, four error styles
95% intervals are Wilson on n = 60

 error style     retried        right field              gave up
 bare          14/60  23.3%   1/60   1.7% [ 0.3,  8.9]  46/60  76.7% [64.6, 85.6]
 traceback      9/60  15.0%   7/60  11.7% [ 5.8, 22.2]  49/60  81.7% [70.1, 89.4]
 vague         22/60  36.7%   2/60   3.3% [ 0.9, 11.4]  38/60  63.3% [50.7, 74.4]
 actionable    60/60 100.0%  60/60 100.0% [94.0,100.0]   0/60   0.0% [ 0.0,  6.0]

 A `valid field` column is not shown because it was identical to `right field`
 in all four conditions: whenever the model recovered far enough to emit one
 of the three legal values, it emitted the correct one. Recovery here is
 all-or-nothing.

 The traceback row does not reconcile: 9 retried plus 49 abandoned is 58, not
 60. Two of that condition's tasks are unaccounted for, so one of its three
 figures is off by up to two tasks. It is flagged rather than quietly patched,
 and re-running that condition is the first thing on this chapter's list.
```

The four strings were:

```text
 bare        "Error"

 traceback   Traceback (most recent call last):
               File "server.py", line 118, in veri_getir
                 return RECORDS[proje][alan]
             KeyError: 'bütçe'

 vague       "HATA: gecersiz alan adi."

 actionable  "HATA: 'bütçe' gecerli bir alan degil.
              Gecerli alanlar sunlardir: butce, personel, sure."
```

The scope of that 100%, stated honestly: the valid set here has three
elements, so the actionable error could list all of it, and a ceiling that
high is close to guaranteed once the model reads it. What this measures is the
*presence* of a recovery instruction, not how well one scales. The interesting
untested case is a set of two hundred values, where all you can offer is the
nearest few — measure that on your own tool before assuming the same jump.

[One sentence took recovery from 1.7% to 100%.]{.hl} The system prompt and the
model were unchanged; the only difference was the text the tool returned on
failure. Which is the section's point rather than an exception to it: that
returned string *is* prompt, written by the tool author instead of the prompt
author.

Three things in that table are worth taking seriously.

**The stack trace is the most interesting of the four, not the worst.** It is
also close to what your tools return today if nobody wrote an error message: a
raw exception. (@sec-agent-anatomy's loop sends back `ERROR: {e}`, which for
this failure is just `ERROR: 'bütçe'` — the traceback's last line, with the
same missing half.) It produced the *fewest* retries — 15.0% against a
bare `"Error"`'s 23.3% — but the retries it produced were the ones that
worked: **7 of its 9 retries landed on the right field, against 1 of 14 for
the bare error and 2 of 22 for the vague one**. Read those as descriptive:
which requests retried at all depended on the error message, so the three
retrying subsets are self-selected and need not be equally hard, and any test
on the conditional rates inherits that. The comparison that holds up is over
all 60 requests, paired. Even so, the pattern fits the three-part rule below
exactly. A
traceback states *what failed* — `KeyError: 'bütçe'` names the offending value
— and says nothing about *what would work*, so it is a half-written error
message, and it behaves like one: rarely acted on, but informative when it is.

What it is *not* is worse than nothing. The abandonment gap that reading rests
on is 49/60 against 46/60 — three tasks, with intervals of [70.1, 89.4] and
[64.6, 85.6]. On the same 60 requests the right test is paired, and even the
most favourable pairing — three requests changing, all in one direction —
gives exact McNemar $p = 0.25$. This experiment cannot resolve that
comparison, and an earlier draft of this chapter called the ordering a result
six separate times. What the four rows *do* separate, unambiguously, is the
actionable string from all three others.

This is the sharpest version of a known result. @huang2024large found that
models cannot reliably correct their own reasoning from *intrinsic* feedback —
being told to try again does not help. What this experiment adds is the
boundary: the same model recovers 1.7% of the time from feedback that carries
no content and 100% of the time from feedback that names the answer set. The
difference is not the model's capacity for self-correction. It is whether the
feedback contains information.

**Giving up is the dominant failure, not looping.** Three of the four styles
produced abandonment in the majority of cases — the model stopped calling tools
and answered without the data. That is worse than a retry loop, which at least
announces itself in the transcript. @sec-agent-anatomy found the opposite
failure, an agent that would not stop; here the same architecture will not
*continue*, and the deciding factor is a sentence.

**"Invalid" is barely better than nothing.** The `vague` style names the
problem in words and still recovered 3.3% of the time. Saying that something is
wrong is not the useful part. Saying what would be right is.

### The rule this gives you

An error message a model can use has three parts, and the last one is the one
that matters:

```text
  1. what failed        'bütçe' is not a valid field
  2. why                (optional; often unnecessary)
  3. what would work    valid fields are: butce, personel, sure
```

Write the third part and the rest is optional. Omit it and you have written a
log line, not a tool.

Two corollaries worth building in:

- **Enumerate the valid options in the error**, exactly as you would in an
  enum. If the set is too large to list, list the nearest few — `did you mean
  butce?` is a complete recovery instruction.
- **Never return a raw exception.** Catch it, and translate. The translation is
  a one-line function and, on this evidence, it bought the largest single
  improvement measured in this chapter.

## What a tool returns is part of its design {#sec-tool-design-results}

A tool's return value goes straight into the transcript, which
@sec-agent-anatomy established *is* the agent's state. So a return value is not
output — it is a write to shared memory that every subsequent step will read
and pay for.

Three rules follow, and all three are routinely broken by tools that were
written for humans first.

**A tool that returns 50,000 tokens has spent a large share of the context
budget in one call.** Whether that breaks the agent depends on the budget and
the task — 50,000 tokens is most of a small window and 5% of a million-token
one, re-sent on every later call — but the costs are the same in either case: context later
steps needed, earlier observations pushed toward the middle where they are used
less well (@sec-context-engineering measures that), and a higher price on every
remaining model call. Return what the *task* needs: the
three fields, not the whole record; the matching rows, not the table.

**Paginate, and say so in the result.** `"showing 10 of 247 matches; call again
with offset=10 for more"` is a sentence the model can act on. Silently
truncating to ten is a tool that lies, and the model has no way to find out.

**Summarise on the tool side when the raw form is unusable.** A tool that
wraps a 40-page PDF should not return 40 pages. What it returns is a design
decision about what the agent is for, and making it inside the tool keeps it
out of every prompt that uses the tool.

**And some things a tool must never return.** Everything a tool returns is
read by the model and, in most products, can end up in front of the user. So a
tool never returns secrets — API keys, passwords, access tokens, internal
connection strings — and never returns records the current user is not
entitled to see; filter by permission *inside* the tool, before the text
reaches the transcript, because the model cannot be trusted to keep a secret it
has read. The reverse direction matters too: text a tool fetches from outside
(a web page, an email, a ticket) is data, not instructions, and a model cannot
reliably tell the two apart. @sec-agent-security treats this as *indirect
prompt injection*; the tool author's part is to mark where fetched text begins
and ends, and never to pass it off as the system's own words.

### Actions need different semantics from lookups

Everything above is about reading. Tools that *do* things need three
properties, and the cheapest time to add them is before the first incident.
They matter most for tools with side effects; the two exceptions after the
table are why "read-only" does not always let you skip them.

| property | why an agent specifically needs it |
|:--|:--|
| **Idempotent** | the same call will arrive twice. A timeout that fires after the action actually succeeded, a run restarted after hitting its step cap, or a model that did not see the result will all produce a second call — and "create the invoice" must not create two |
| **Dry-run mode** | lets the agent, or you, see the effect before committing to it. A first-class `dry_run: true` parameter is worth more than any amount of prompt instruction |
| **Confirmation-gated** | some actions should not execute on a model's say-so at all. That gate belongs in the runtime, not the prompt — @sec-guardrails is where this becomes a chapter |

: Three properties a writing tool needs {tbl-colwidths="[26,74]"}

The first row has a name worth knowing:
[**idempotency**](#gloss-idempotency){#term-idempotency .term-ref}. A call is
idempotent when making it twice has the same effect as making it once. Reads
are idempotent by nature; "set the status to *paid*" is too; "add 100 TL to
the balance" is not. The standard way to make a writing call idempotent is an
*idempotency key*: the runtime attaches a unique id to each intended action,
and the tool remembers which ids it has already carried out, so a repeat
returns the first result instead of acting again.

::: {#gloss-idempotency .column-margin .term-gloss}
**idempotency** — a call that can be repeated without repeating its effect;
what makes a retried agent step safe.
[↩](#term-idempotency){.term-back}
:::

A read-only tool can usually skip all three, with two exceptions worth naming:
a read that costs real money per call still wants a dry run, and a read over
data the user may not be entitled to still wants a gate. "Read-only" bounds the
damage; it does not always make the call free or harmless.

The general principle is @sec-agent-anatomy's, restated for the tool author:
the model emits arguments and the runtime decides. Anything you would not let
an unreviewed pull request do automatically, do not let a tool call do
automatically.

## Scaling past fifty tools {#sec-tool-design-scale}

The previous section was about what one tool puts into the context when it is
called. This one is about what the tools cost *before* any of them is called.

Every tool definition sits in the context of every call, so a flat list of
fifty tools is a large fixed tax on every step, paid whether or not any of them
is relevant. The published figures are larger than most people expect:
@anthropic2025advancedtools reports a catalogue of 50-plus tools whose
definitions alone cost about **72,000 tokens** — some **77,000** with the rest
of the starting context — before a single call, and an **85% reduction** from
loading definitions on demand. @sec-mcp measures what the same tax looks like
once your tools arrive over a protocol rather than out of your own codebase.

It also gets *less* accurate — more near-duplicate options means more chances
to pick a neighbouring one — and the same report puts numbers on that too:
tool-selection accuracy on a large surface rose from **49% to 74%** for one
model, and from 79.5% to 88.1% for a stronger one, purely by searching the
catalogue instead of pasting it in. That is the unusual case where the cheap
fix and the accurate fix are the same fix.

Three ways out, in increasing order of how much they change your architecture:

- **Namespace and prune.** Large tool surfaces often contain two or three
  tools that do the same thing for historical reasons. Merging them is free
  accuracy. The same instinct sets a tool's *granularity*: build one tool per
  task a user has, not one per endpoint of your API — a single
  `schedule_meeting` rather than `list_users`, `list_events` and
  `create_event`, which the model would have to chain correctly on its own.
- **Search, then load** —
  [**progressive disclosure**](#gloss-progressive-disclosure){#term-progressive-disclosure .term-ref}.
  Expose one `find_tools(query)` and load only the matching definitions for
  that step. This is @sec-retrieval applied to your
  own API surface, and it is what @anthropic2025advancedtools ships as a
  first-class API feature. The threshold at which to reach for it is not a
  constant. Anthropic's documentation says selection accuracy degrades once a
  model sees more than about 30–50 tools, and suggests search from as few as
  ten tools or 10,000 tokens of definitions; verbose definitions reach that
  sooner. Measure your own definition tax before picking a number.
- **Give it an interpreter instead.** If your tools are mostly small
  transformations, a sandboxed code environment replaces fifty definitions
  with one — the model composes what it needs rather than picking from a menu.

::: {#gloss-progressive-disclosure .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Progressive disclosure** — loading only the tool definitions relevant to the
current step instead of all of them, so a large surface does not tax every
call. [↩](#term-progressive-disclosure){.term-back}
:::

### Code mode, and what it costs

That third option — [**code mode**](#gloss-code-mode){#term-code-mode .term-ref}
— deserves naming clearly, because providers now ship it:
Cloudflare's Code Mode [@cloudflare2025codemode] and Anthropic's *programmatic
tool calling* [@anthropic2025advancedtools] both let the model write code that
calls the tools, instead of calling them one round-trip at a time.

::: {#gloss-code-mode .column-margin .term-gloss}
**Code mode** — giving an agent a sandboxed interpreter instead of a fixed
tool list. Composition, loops and intermediate variables come free; a readable
whitelist does not. [↩](#term-code-mode){.term-back}
:::

Instead of `filter_rows`, `sum_column` and
`join_tables`, you expose a sandbox and let the model write the composition.
It is genuinely more expressive: composition, loops and intermediate variables
come free, and they are exactly what a fixed tool list makes awkward.

The cost is that [you have replaced a whitelist with an interpreter]{.hl}. A
tool list is a security boundary you can read; a sandbox is a security boundary
you have to build and keep believing in. That is a real trade and it belongs to
@sec-agent-security rather than to a paragraph here — but the design decision
is made in this chapter, when you choose what surface to expose.

## Evaluating a tool {#sec-tool-design-eval}

A tool is not correct because it works. It has to be right on two counts: the
model has to **call it right**, which is a property of the pair and can only be
measured by asking, and the tool has to **do the right thing when called
right** — return the correct result, and no side effect nobody asked for. This
section is about the first, because it is the one tool authors skip; do not let
that stand in for the ordinary tests you would write for any other function.

The evaluation is small enough to build in an afternoon and it is the same
shape as this chapter's two experiments:

1. **Collect twenty real requests** that should reach this tool, phrased the
   way users phrase them rather than the way your API is named. This is where
   the misuse hides.
2. **Score the call, not the outcome.** Was the right tool chosen; are the
   arguments right? Executing muddles a schema problem with everything
   downstream — the schema experiment above deliberately executed nothing.
3. **Count the three failure kinds separately**, because they have different
   fixes:

| failure | what it means | what fixes it |
|:--|:--|:--|
| **Not called** | the model answered without the tool, or picked a neighbour | the *name*, and the description's "use this when" |
| **Called wrong** | right tool, wrong arguments | types and enums, then parameter descriptions |
| **Not recovered** | a failed call the model could not act on | the error string |

: Three failure kinds, three different fixes {tbl-colwidths="[20,44,36]"}

4. **Add the twenty requests to your regression set.** A tool description is
   prompt text, so changing it is a change to system behaviour and deserves the
   same treatment as changing a prompt — @sec-llm-eval sized how many items you
   need before a difference means anything.

The "not called" row is the one worth instrumenting in production, because it
is invisible otherwise. A tool that is never selected produces no errors and no
logs; it just quietly does not participate, while the model answers from memory
— which is exactly what the opaque schema did, 41.7% of the time, in prose that
looked like an answer.

## Intuition checks {#sec-tool-design-intuition}

Answer each one before you open it. Four are questions this chapter settled
with a measurement rather than an argument; the other two are design decisions
it argues for and cannot measure.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Where should you spend your time on a tool schema?

On enums, before prose. Measured here, moving one parameter from a free string
to an enumerated list took correct calls from **25% to 100%**, and adding
careful descriptions on top added nothing observable. Be exact about why: the
runtime here did not enforce the enum, so listing the values supplied
vocabulary the model followed, and the experiment never tested prose without
the enum. A decoder that *does* enforce it guarantees only that the value is in
the set — not that it is the right one.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Your tool has a badly named, undocumented schema. What is the failure?

Usually not a wrong call — **no call**. With an opaque schema the model here
invoked the tool only 58.3% of the time and otherwise answered from parametric
memory, producing a confident paragraph about something it could not know. A
wrong call raises an error you can see; an unused tool produces a plausible
answer and no signal at all.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Why does a model pass "mali buyukluk" where your API wants "butce"?

Because nothing told it otherwise, so it echoes the user's vocabulary into your
parameter. In this chapter's measurement only two phrasings worked, and neither contains
the API's word: the model mapped their meaning onto a field name and landed on
the API's own. One case
is worth noticing specially: the model wrote `bütçe` where the API expects
`butce` — correct Turkish, wrong identifier, and a failure waiting inside any
API whose values are ASCII-folded words.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. What should a tool return when it fails?

What would have worked. Measured across four styles, recovery went from **1.7%
to 100%** purely by naming the invalid value and listing the valid ones. The
striking row is the stack trace: it produced the fewest retries of the four,
because it names the value that failed and never what would have worked. It is
a half-written error message, not a worse-than-nothing one — the abandonment
gap against a bare `"Error"` is three tasks in sixty and does not survive a
test. Catch it and add the missing sentence.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. A tool returns the full record — 8,000 tokens. Is that a problem?

Yes, and it is a problem for the whole run rather than that step. The return
value goes into the transcript, which @sec-agent-anatomy showed *is* the
agent's state, so it is re-sent on every subsequent model call and it crowds
out what later steps need. Return the fields the task needs, paginate with the
pagination stated in the result, and summarise on the tool side when the raw
form is unusable.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. When do you stop adding tools and expose an interpreter instead?

When the tools are mostly small transformations that users want to *compose* —
filter, then sum, then join — because composition is exactly what a fixed list
makes awkward and what code makes free. Be explicit about the price: you have
replaced a whitelist you can read with a sandbox you have to build and keep
trusting. That is a security decision made in this chapter and paid for in
@sec-agent-security.
:::

## Interview questions {#sec-tool-design-interview}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**On sourcing — the same caveat as @sec-text-as-data.** These recur in the two
credible open sources this book uses, plus the ones this chapter's own
measurements make answerable.
:::

### Testing whether you understand the mechanism

**Q: What makes a good tool schema?**

Start from the framing that decides everything else: the schema is prompt text,
not documentation, because the model gets one shot from it with no way to check.
Then order the work by effect. Enums first — measured here, enumerating one
parameter took correct calls from 25% to 100% while prose descriptions on top
added nothing. Then a name that says *when* the tool applies. Then parameter
descriptions written as a mapping from users' words to your API's words,
because otherwise the model passes the user's vocabulary straight through.

**Q: Your agent ignores a tool that would answer the question. Why?**

Most likely the name and description do not say when it applies, so the model
does not recognise the situation as this tool's. The important half of the
answer is what that failure looks like: not an error, but an answer from
parametric memory. In this chapter's measurement an opaque schema went uncalled
41.7% of the time and produced confident invented prose instead. So instrument
*selection*, not just failures.

**Q: What should a tool return on error?**

A sentence saying what would have worked, with the valid options enumerated.
Measured across four styles, that took recovery from 1.7% to 100%. And say the
counterintuitive part, because it is the useful one: a stack trace produced the
*fewest* retries of the four, because it names the value that failed and never
what would work. It is a half-written error message, not a worse-than-nothing
one — its abandonment gap against a bare "Error" is three tasks in sixty and
does not survive a test. Catch the exception and add the missing sentence.

### Testing whether you have shipped one

**Q: How do you evaluate a tool?**

By whether the model calls it correctly, which is a property of the pair. Twenty
requests in users' phrasing, scored on the emitted call rather than the outcome
so a schema problem is not confounded with everything downstream, bucketed into
not-called, called-wrong and not-recovered — because those have three different
fixes. Then keep the twenty in the regression set, since a description change is
a behaviour change. Say what this does not cover: it measures the model–tool
interface, and the tool's own implementation and side effects need testing
separately, like any other function.

**Q: You have eighty tools and accuracy is falling. What do you do?**

First merge and prune, because large surfaces accumulate near-duplicates and
every extra near-neighbour is another chance to pick the wrong one. Then move
from a flat list to search-then-load, so only the relevant definitions occupy
the context — @sec-retrieval applied to your own API. If the tools are mostly
small composable transformations, consider replacing them with a sandboxed
interpreter, and be explicit that you are trading a readable whitelist for a
security boundary you now have to maintain.

## Lab: fix a tool by measuring it {#sec-tool-design-lab}

Six steps, one afternoon, and the point of the sequence is that you change one
thing at a time — so that at the end you can say which change bought what.

### Step 1 — pick a tool the model gets wrong

If you do not know which one, you have found the first task: log tool calls
with their arguments for a day.

### Step 2 — write twenty requests in users' words

Not in your API's words. The gap between the two is the thing being measured.

### Step 3 — score the call, executing nothing

Right tool, right arguments, both or neither. Record the baseline.

### Step 4 — change one thing: add enums

Every parameter with a fixed value set. Re-measure. On this chapter's tool that
single change was worth 75 percentage points (25% to 100%).

### Step 5 — now rewrite the descriptions

Re-measure again. Report the delta honestly, including if it is zero, as it was
here.

### Step 6 — break it on purpose and fix the error string

Force a failing call. Try the bare error, then the actionable one. Count how
often the model recovers.

### What to hand in

The four-row table of your own — baseline, enums, descriptions, error string —
and one sentence saying which change you would have predicted was largest, and
whether you were right.

## Exercises {#sec-tool-design-exercises}

1. **The enum sweep.** Take one tool with a free-string parameter that has a
   fixed value set. Measure correct calls, add the enum, measure again. Report
   both numbers.
2. **Users' words, not yours.** Write twenty requests for one of your tools in
   the vocabulary your users actually use. Count how many produce the right
   arguments. The gap is your parameter descriptions' job.
3. **Rewrite the worst error.** Find the ugliest error string a tool of yours
   can return. Rewrite it in the three-part form. Measure recovery before and
   after.
4. **Find the silent tool.** Instrument which tools are never selected. For
   each one, decide whether it is redundant or badly named — both are fixable,
   and both are invisible without the instrumentation.
5. **Budget a return value.** Take a tool that returns a whole record and
   compute what it costs across a ten-step run. Then decide what it should
   return instead.
6. **Dry-run.** Add a `dry_run` parameter to a tool that writes something.
   Measure whether the agent uses it when asked to be careful, and whether the
   instruction is even necessary once the parameter exists.
7. **The ASCII trap.** If your API uses ASCII-folded identifiers derived from
   words in a language with diacritics, write the test that catches
   `bütçe`/`butce` before a user does.

## Where to go deeper {#sec-tool-design-deeper}

Do this before reading anything: take one tool, add enums to every parameter
that has a fixed value set, and measure the change. It is twenty minutes.

| [Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents) — Anthropic | the surrounding argument: what to build before you need tools at all |
| [`pydantic-ai`](https://github.com/pydantic/pydantic-ai) | tools as typed functions, with validation errors that are already model-readable — the error-message finding, built in |

## What to remember {#sec-tool-design-summary}

- **A tool schema is prompt text, not documentation.** The model gets one shot
  from it, cannot read your source, and cannot check a guess. Whatever the
  schema does not say, it invents.
- **Enumerate before you describe.** Moving one parameter from a free string
  to an enumerated list took correct calls from **25% to 100%**; prose on top
  added nothing observable once the enum had reached 60/60. Prose *without* an
  enum was not tested, and for parameters you cannot enumerate it is the only
  bridge you have.
- **A bad schema produces no call, not a wrong call.** The opaque variant went
  uncalled **41.7%** of the time and answered from parametric memory instead —
  a confident invented paragraph, which is worse than an error because it looks
  like an answer.
- **Without constraints the model echoes the user's vocabulary into your API.**
  *mali buyukluk*, *ekip mevcudu*, *takvim* — and `bütçe` where the API wanted
  `butce`, which is @sec-turkish-nlp's problem arriving inside a function
  signature.
- **The error string made the largest single difference measured here.** Recovery
  went from **1.7% to 100%** by naming the invalid value and listing the valid
  ones. Write what *would* have worked; the rest is optional.
- **A stack trace is a half-written error message.** It names the value that
  failed and never what would have worked, so it produced the fewest retries
  of any style — though, of the three incomplete styles, its retries were the
  most often correct, 7 of 9. Do not read it as *worse than nothing*: at n = 60 that comparison sits
  inside the noise. Read it as unfinished, and add the third sentence.
- **The dominant failure after an error is giving up, not looping.** Three of
  four error styles made the model stop calling tools and answer without the
  data — a quieter failure than a retry loop and a worse one.
- **What a tool returns is a write to the agent's state.** Return the fields
  the task needs, state the pagination in the result, and summarise on the tool
  side. A 50,000-token result can consume context later steps need and is
  carried into every later call; judge it against the task's context and cost
  budgets. Never return secrets or records the user may not see.
- **A tool that acts must survive being called twice.** Make it idempotent,
  give it a dry run, and put the confirmation gate in the runtime, not the
  prompt.
